title: Entertaining angels (Hebrews 13:1–2)

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith: the substance of things hoped for, and a family list that isn't closed. Your line was faith is the substance.

The hottest part of the day. An old man sits at the door of his tent, under the oaks of Mamre, and looks up to see three strangers standing nearby. He doesn't wait to find out who they are. He runs to meet them, bows to the ground, and has bread baked and a calf prepared while they rest in the shade. That's Abraham in Genesis eighteen, and by the end of the visit it's clear these were no ordinary travelers. Centuries later, in the last chapter of Hebrews, among a few short pieces of advice, the writer reaches back for that afternoon.
screen: `THREE STRANGERS AT MAMRE.` → `ABRAHAM RUNS TO MEET THEM.` → `HEBREWS REMEMBERS THAT AFTERNOON.`

segments.voice: Chapter thirteen puts two kinds of love side by side: love for the family of believers, and love for people you don't know at all. The Douay-Rheims puts it this way: "And hospitality do not forget; for by this some, being not aware of it, have entertained angels." The King James Bible ends the verse with the phrase in today's line: angels unawares. The Greek word behind hospitality is philoxenia, simply love of strangers. Not love of guests you invited; love of the person you didn't expect. Hebrews names no one here, but readers often think of stories like these. Abraham at Mamre, feeding three visitors. Lot, taking two strangers into his house in Sodom. And Catholic Bibles hold another, in the book of Tobias: a young man sets out on a long journey with a hired companion who calls himself Azarias, and only at the very end does the companion reveal that he is the angel Raphael. A whole road trip, and nobody knew. Notice what Hebrews doesn't say. It doesn't promise that every stranger is an angel, or tell you to be kind in case one is. The point runs the other way: you can't sort people in advance, so welcome everyone. Jesus says it even more directly in Matthew twenty-five: "I was a stranger, and you took me in." Saint Benedict wrote it into his rule for monks: every guest who comes to the door is to be received as Christ himself.
screen: `PHILOXENIA: LOVE OF STRANGERS.` · `ABRAHAM, LOT, TOBIAS AND RAPHAEL.` · `YOU CAN'T SORT PEOPLE IN ADVANCE.` · `I WAS A STRANGER, AND YOU TOOK ME IN.` · then, large: `ANGELS UNAWARES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone new to a place you know: a new face at work or at church, a family that just moved onto your street. Picture them at the edge of the room, then picture yourself crossing it to greet them and making room for them at the table, and let that feel ordinary. If you pray, hold the line I was a stranger, and you took me in; if not, just hold the face kindly.
Entertaining angels. Hebrews thirteen: welcome strangers, because some, without knowing it, have welcomed angels. Today's word.
Your line: angels unawares. Love for the person you didn't expect at the door. James is next.

howItsDone: Catholic parishes, religious houses and charities practice hospitality to strangers, from welcoming newcomers at Mass to meals and shelter for travelers and the homeless, and Benedictine monasteries still receive guests as Christ, following the Rule of Saint Benedict.
